reasoning_notes.reasoning: With no history, a midpoint wage balances margin and the chance of winning labor.
With equal revenue and no history, a middle wage balances winning labor against margin; avoid bidding near the zero-profit maximum.
Undercut B by one to win the unit; profit is 11 instead of 5 if B repeats 10.
Matching A’s previous wage splits the unit evenly and earns 5, while undercutting sacrifices profit per unit.
B's last winning offer was 10; matching it splits labor for profit 5, while undercutting further sacrifices margin. A higher offer loses the unit.
Matching 10 preserves the current winning offer and avoids sacrificing margin to undercut; A may respond, but 10 remains a profitable tie.
Matching B’s repeated 10 offer earns half the unit for profit 5; undercutting to 9 earned nothing. A higher offer would win the unit but reduce profit below 5.
Matching 10 preserves a 50% share and profit of 5; undercutting sacrifices margin, while raising above 10 risks losing the round's profit.
B has repeatedly offered 10; matching earns A 5, while undercutting loses the unit. With the final round unknown, keep matching the profitable offer.

Matching A's consistent 10 secures half the labor for profit 5; undercutting by 1 would win all labor but yield profit 9, yet risks provoking a wage response. With an unknown horizon, maintain the profitable match.
B has repeatedly offered 10, so matching preserves a half share and earns 5; a higher wage would reduce profit if B stays at 10.
A has repeatedly matched 10, so matching preserves half the labor and earns 5 while avoiding a costly wage increase.
Matching the recurring wage of 10 preserves a 5 profit if tied; undercutting gives up margin, while a higher wage loses money if matched.
Matching the observed 10 wage shares labor while earning positive profit; higher wages reduce margin, and undercutting risks losing the share if rivals stay at 10.

At 10, three-way matching yields profit 3⅓. Undercutting to 9 captures all labor for profit 11, while a higher wage loses the pool. With no disclosed final round, taking the profitable undercut is best.
Matching the established 10 wage preserves a chance at labor without paying more; undercutting risks losing the tie advantage and lowering profit per unit.
Matching the established 10 offer preserves a profitable share; undercutting risks earning less overall.
At 9 I earned nothing because both rivals offered 10. Matching 10 secures a one-third share if C also matches, while undercutting again risks zero against the two firms at 10.
Both rivals have stayed at 10; matching preserves half the labor and earns 5, while undercutting them would reduce profit per unit.
Matching the established offer earns a positive share; undercutting sacrifices margin, while raising risks losing all labor.
Matching the established wage earns a positive one-third share; undercutting to 9 failed to win labor last time.
Both rivals offered 10 last round. Matching preserves a one-third share at a positive margin; undercutting would sacrifice profit, while bidding above 10 costs more without a clear gain.
Matching the established offer earns a profitable share; undercutting sacrifices margin, while a higher offer reduces profit if it wins.
Matching 10 shares the unit profitably with firms that also bid 10; undercutting to 9 previously earned nothing, and bidding above 10 lowers profit if I win.
Matching 10 preserves the established tie; undercutting sacrifices revenue per unit, while raising the wage gives up profit if matched.
